title: The poisoned arrow
hook: the Buddha: a wounded man won't wait to learn who shot him before the arrow comes out (Majjhima Nikaya 63)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kisa Gotami went door to door for the mustard seed. Your line was no house without it. Were you gentle with someone's grief, or your own? Day seventy-six.

Something goes wrong. The deal falls through, the diagnosis comes back, the text you didn't want arrives. And right away your mind fills with questions. Why did this happen? Whose fault is it? What does it mean about my life? Was it always going to go this way? Those questions can go all night. Some of them matter. But while they're spinning, the actual hurt is still sitting there, untouched. The Buddha had a picture for this, and it's one of the sharpest in all of his teaching. Today's story is the poisoned arrow.
screen: `SOMETHING GOES WRONG.` → `WHY? WHOSE FAULT?` → `THE HURT, STILL UNTOUCHED.`

segments.voice: It's in the Middle Length Discourses, the Majjhima Nikaya, number sixty-three. A monk named Malunkyaputta is sitting alone and stewing. There are big questions the Buddha has never answered. Is the universe eternal, or not? Is it infinite, or not? Is the soul the same as the body? What happens to an awakened one after death? So he goes to the Buddha and gives him an ultimatum: answer these, or I'm leaving. The Buddha's reply starts with a question of his own: did I ever promise you I'd answer them? And then he tells a story. Imagine a man shot with an arrow thickly smeared with poison. His friends and family rush to bring a surgeon. But the man says: I won't let anyone pull this arrow out until I know who shot me. Was he a noble, a priest, a merchant, a worker? What was his name, and his family? Was he tall or short, dark or fair? What village did he come from? Was the bow a longbow or a crossbow? What was the string made of? What feathers were on the arrow? And the Buddha says: that man would die before he learned any of it. The questions Malunkyaputta asked aren't foolish, he says; they just don't lead to peace. What he teaches instead is suffering, where it comes from, its ending, and the path to that ending. In other words: the wound, and how to heal it. Buddhists have discussed for centuries what the Buddha's silence on those questions means, and they don't all agree. But the order in the story is clear. First, the arrow comes out. The questions can come after, if they still seem urgent.
screen: `MALUNKYAPUTTA'S ULTIMATUM.` · `A MAN SHOT WITH A POISONED ARROW.` · `WHO SHOT ME? WHAT BOW?` · `FIRST THE WOUND, THEN THE QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `PULL THE ARROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pull one arrow instead of asking why. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that's hurting a little today, not the biggest thing, just one. Notice the why questions that come with it: whose fault, what it means, how it happened. Set them to one side for now; they'll keep. Then ask a smaller question: what would help this hurt, right now? A glass of water, an apology, a walk, a phone call, a rest. Find one. Picture doing it. The bell holds the time.
The poisoned arrow. The Buddha's picture of a wounded man who wants every answer before he'll let the surgeon help. Today's word.
Your line: pull the arrow. Today, when something stings, do the one thing that helps before you ask whose fault it was. Day seventy-six.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the parable of the poisoned arrow to explain why the Buddha set aside certain metaphysical questions and focused on suffering and its ending.

let him go without a word
fork.reveal: he asks whether he ever promised to answer those questions, then tells of a man shot with a poisoned arrow who dies waiting to learn who shot him.

original.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: salla, an arrow or dart, the word for the barb in the Buddha's picture.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha didn't want people asking hard questions.
what it means: some questions don't lead to peace; first heal the wound in front of you.
what a scholar hears: the Culamalunkya Sutta (MN 63) and the undeclared questions, which Buddhists still discuss.

notes: Sutta paraphrased. Confirm the list of questions (the ten undeclared points, here abridged to four) and the details the wounded man demands (caste, name, clan, height, complexion, village, bow, string, shaft, feathers).
Pali salla (सल्ल) for the arrow: confirm the word used in MN 63 (sallena viddho).
The script says Buddhists do not all agree on what the silence means; a Buddhist scholar may want to confirm this is fairly put.
